hook.text: Habitat loss is the number one driver of extinction. It isn't even close.

buildup.text: Forests become farms. Wetlands become malls. Grasslands become suburbs.

discovery.text: When habitat fragments, small isolated populations lose genetic diversity and die out.

twist.text: Wildlife corridors — strips of habitat connecting fragments — can prevent that collapse.

climax.text: We have converted over 75% of ice-free land for human use. Only 25% remains wild.

punchline.text: Species don't go extinct in the wild. The wild goes extinct around them.

quiz.question: What is the leading cause of species extinction?

details.summary: Habitat destruction from agriculture, urbanization, and resource extraction is the leading cause of biodiversity loss worldwide. Converting forests, wetlands, and grasslands eliminates the resources species need to survive, feed, and reproduce.
details.whyItMatters: No conservation effort succeeds if habitat keeps disappearing. Protecting and restoring habitat is the single most effective action for preserving biodiversity.
takeaways: Agriculture is the largest driver of habitat conversion globally
Fragmentation isolates populations and reduces genetic exchange
Wetland loss exceeds 85 percent in many regions since 1700

faq.question: How much natural habitat has humanity destroyed?
faq.answer: Humans have transformed roughly 75 percent of ice-free land surface, converting forests, wetlands, and grasslands into farmland, cities, and infrastructure. Only about 23 percent of land still functions as a relatively intact ecosystem.

faq.question: What is habitat fragmentation and why is it harmful?
faq.answer: Fragmentation breaks continuous habitat into small, isolated patches surrounded by human land uses. Small populations in fragments face inbreeding, cannot migrate, and are more vulnerable to disease, storms, and local extinction.
